71.title: Rabia's torch and bucket
71.hook: Rabia of Basra carries fire to burn paradise and water to drown hell, so God is loved for God alone (Attar, Memorial of the Saints)
71.howItsDone: Sufis honor Rabia al-Adawiyya as an early teacher of love for God for God's own sake, and her story and sayings are told in Sufi gatherings and books of saints.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the cicada sang all summer while the ants stored grain and shut the door, an ending people still argue over. Your line was store, and share.

A woman is hurrying through the streets of Basra, in what's now Iraq. In one hand, a burning torch. In the other, a bucket of water, sloshing as she goes. People stop and stare. Finally someone asks the obvious question: where are you going with those? Her answer is still told. It opens a new week of homes: Sufi teachers, desert monks, and the Buddha.
screen: `A WOMAN IN THE STREETS OF BASRA.` → `A TORCH IN ONE HAND.` → `WATER IN THE OTHER.`

segments.voice: Rabia al-Adawiyya of Basra is remembered among the early Sufis, the teachers of the inner, mystical path within Islam. Most of what we know comes from writers who lived long after her, especially the Persian poet Attar, in his Memorial of the Saints. So these are stories told about her, and scholars read them that way. Tradition says she was born poor, sold into slavery as a girl, and set free after her master saw her praying through the night. When people ask what the torch and bucket are for, she says, as the story is told: I'm going to set fire to paradise and pour water on the fires of hell, so that both are gone. Then people will worship God not out of fear of punishment, not out of hope for a reward, but for God alone. It's meant to startle. Rabia isn't mocking heaven or hell; she's asking what's underneath our reasons. If the reward vanished, and the threat vanished, would the love still be there? Another saying people attribute to her makes the same point: she wanted to love God for God's own beauty, not as a bargain. You don't have to share her faith to feel the edge of that question. So much of what we do comes with a receipt attached: the praise, the payback, the good review. But there's another kind. A parent rocking a baby at three in the morning. Someone singing alone in the car. Nobody's keeping score. That's the love Rabia was walking through Basra for.
screen: `RABIA OF BASRA, AN EARLY SUFI.` · `BURN PARADISE, DROWN HELL.` · `NO FEAR, NO REWARD — GOD ALONE.` · `LOVE WITHOUT A RECEIPT.` · then, large: `FOR ITS OWN SAKE.`

segments.voice: Think of something good you did recently, and notice honestly what you hoped to get back: thanks, a good impression, a favor later, with no blame. Then picture one small good thing you could do that nobody will ever know about, picture no one noticing, and see how that feels. If you pray, you might simply sit with Rabia's question in silence.
Rabia. An early Sufi teacher who carried fire for paradise and water for hell, so that what was left was love for its own sake.
Your line: for its own sake. What's left, with no reward and no threat, is love. See you tomorrow.

72.title: The elephant in the dark
72.hook: people touch an elephant in a dark room and call it a fan, a pillar, a throne (Rumi, Masnavi 3.1259ff)
72.tomorrow: Abba Moses and the leaking basket
72.howItsDone: Readers of Rumi's Masnavi often tell the elephant in the dark when talking about the limits of what any one person perceives, and teachers in many settings use it to open conversations across disagreement.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabia carried fire for paradise and water for hell, so God would be loved for God alone. Your line was for its own sake.

Think of a family argument about something that happened years ago. Your sister remembers one thing, your dad another, and you remember a third, and you'd swear to it. Everyone was there. Everyone is sure. And somehow nobody's lying: each of you touched a different part of the same afternoon. The Persian poet Rumi, writing in the twelve hundreds, told a story about exactly this, set in a dark room, with a very large visitor inside.
screen: `EVERYONE WAS THERE.` → `EVERYONE IS SURE.` → `A DARK ROOM, A LARGE VISITOR.`

segments.voice: It's in his long poem, the Masnavi, in its third book. Travelers bring an elephant to a town where no one has ever seen one, and keep it in a dark house. People crowd in, but it's too dark to see, so each one reaches out and touches. One hand finds the trunk: this creature is like a water pipe. Another finds the ear: no, it's like a fan. Another wraps her arms around a leg: it's a pillar. Another pats the back: it's shaped like a throne. Each description is honest, each is about something real, and each is wrong about the whole. Then comes the line the story turns on. If each of them had held a candle, Rumi says, the difference would have gone out of their words. Nobody needed to shout louder. They needed light. Rumi was a Muslim scholar and Sufi teacher, and he uses the story to say something about the limits of our senses: the hand can only know what it touches. Readers have taken it in many directions since, and people disagree about how far to push it. An older cousin of the story appears in the Buddhist Udana, where a king has blind men describe an elephant, and they end up in a fistfight. So the picture has traveled. When someone describes something completely differently from you, maybe one of you is simply wrong. Or maybe you've got the ear, and they've got the leg. Before arguing, ask what their hand is touching.
screen: `AN ELEPHANT IN A DARK HOUSE.` · `A PIPE, A FAN, A PILLAR, A THRONE.` · `WITH A CANDLE, NO DIFFERENCE.` · `ASK WHAT THEIR HAND IS TOUCHING.` · then, large: `BRING A CANDLE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a person who sees some small, real matter differently from you, and picture the two of you in the dark room, each with a hand on the elephant. Ask yourself gently: what part might they be touching that I'm not? Then picture asking them one honest question that begins, how do you see it?
Masnavi. Rumi's long poem, where hands in a dark room each touch an elephant, each honest, each partial, until a candle could have ended the argument.
Your line: bring a candle. Every hand in the dark is honest, and only partly right. Day seventy-two, done.

73.title: Abba Moses and the leaking basket
73.hook: asked to judge a brother, he arrives carrying a basket leaking sand: my own faults run out behind me (Sayings of the Desert Fathers)
73.howItsDone: The Sayings of the Desert Fathers are read in Orthodox, Coptic, Catholic and some Protestant communities, and Abba Moses is honored as a saint; the leaking basket is often told when people talk about not judging.

segments.voice: Yesterday, from Rumi's Masnavi: hands in the dark found a pipe, a fan, a pillar and a throne, and a candle would have ended the argument. Your line was bring a candle.

Someone messes up, and the group chat lights up. Did you hear what he did? Can you believe she said that? It's a strange kind of fun, deciding together how wrong someone else was. Now move the scene to the Egyptian desert. A community of early Christian monks has gathered to sit in judgment on one of their brothers. They're waiting for one more elder, a big, famous old man named Moses. And when he finally walks in, he's carrying something odd.
screen: `DID YOU HEAR WHAT HE DID?` → `THE MONKS GATHER TO JUDGE.` → `ONE ELDER IS LATE.`

segments.voice: Early Christian monks went out into the deserts of Egypt to live simply and pray. They called their elders abba, father, and the elders' short, sharp sayings were later written down as the Sayings of the Desert Fathers, still read in monasteries today. Abba Moses is a surprise among them. Tradition says he came from Ethiopia, was once a servant and then the leader of a gang of robbers, before he turned up at a monastery and slowly became one of its gentlest elders. At the settlement of Scetis, a brother does something wrong. The monks call a council and send for Moses. He doesn't want to come. They send again: everyone is waiting for you. So he goes, carrying a container full of holes, with something running out behind him the whole way. In the Greek sayings, it's a jug, leaking water; later retellings make it a basket, trickling sand. The monks come out to meet him and ask: father, what is this? And Moses says, more or less: my own faults are running out behind me, and I don't even see them, and today I've come to judge somebody else's. That's all. The story says the monks said nothing more to the brother, and forgave him. He doesn't say the brother did nothing wrong. He doesn't give a speech about mercy. He walks in carrying the truth about himself where everyone can see it, and the room changes. The trail behind him is the whole sermon.
screen: `THE DESERT FATHERS OF EGYPT.` · `MOSES, ONCE A ROBBER.` · `A CONTAINER FULL OF HOLES.` · `MY FAULTS RUN OUT BEHIND ME.` · then, large: `MY OWN BASKET LEAKS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you've been quietly judging, a coworker, a relative, a stranger online, and just notice the judgment without arguing with it. Now picture walking toward them carrying Moses's basket, a thin line of sand running out behind you: a few of your own old mistakes, the ones you'd rather nobody mentioned. You don't have to drop the judgment; carry the basket alongside it, and feel what happens.
Scetis. The desert settlement where an elder came to a trial carrying his own faults behind him, in a basket that leaked the whole way.
Your line: my own basket leaks. The judge carries faults too, whether he sees them or not. That's day seventy-three.

74.title: Become all flame
74.hook: Abba Lot asks what more he can do, and Abba Joseph raises fingers like lamps: why not become all flame? (Sayings of the Desert Fathers)
74.howItsDone: Monks and other Christians, especially in the Orthodox tradition, read Abba Joseph's saying as a call to be transformed by God completely; lighting a candle before prayer is a common practice in Orthodox and Catholic churches.

segments.voice: Yesterday, at Scetis, Abba Moses walked into a trial with his own faults running out behind him. Your line was my own basket leaks.

Say the good habits are built. The streak is going. You drink the water, take the walk, sit with the bell most days. And one evening a small question slips in: is this it? Is there something more, and what is it? It's not a complaint. It's a real question, and people have asked it for a very long time. In the Egyptian desert, a monk named Lot asked it out loud, to an older monk named Joseph. And Joseph answered without a single instruction.
screen: `THE HABITS ARE GOING.` → `IS THIS IT?` → `LOT ASKS JOSEPH.`

segments.voice: It's another story from the Sayings of the Desert Fathers, the same collection as yesterday's leaking basket. Abba Lot visits Abba Joseph and lays out his life honestly. As far as I can, he says, I keep my little rule of prayer. I fast a little. I pray, and I keep quiet. As far as I can, I keep my thoughts clean. What else should I do? It's a humble list, and notice the phrase he keeps using: as far as I can. Joseph doesn't criticize any of it. He stands up and stretches his hands toward heaven, and the story says his fingers became like ten lamps of fire. And he says to Lot: if you want, you can become all flame. That's the end of the saying. The collection doesn't tell us what Lot did next. For the desert monks, the answer to what more should I do was not another item on the list. The list is good; the list is the fuel. But the point was never to finish it. It was to be changed by what the list was for, all the way through. In Christian teaching, especially in the Orthodox tradition, the saying is read as the life of God filling a person completely, a person transformed by God's light. If you don't share that faith, the picture still speaks. There's a difference between doing a practice and being lit by it, between saying the words and meaning them with your whole self. Joseph didn't say pray more. He said: burn.
screen: `WHAT ELSE SHOULD I DO?` · `LOT'S HONEST, HUMBLE LIST.` · `FINGERS LIKE TEN LAMPS.` · `THE LIST IS THE FUEL, NOT THE POINT.` · then, large: `ALL FLAME.`

segments.voice: If you have a candle and a safe place for it, light it now; if not, a lamp will do, or picture one clearly. Watch the flame: it isn't one still thing, it moves, and it doesn't do fire partly. When your mind starts a list, come back to the flame, and if you pray, hold Joseph's words in silence.
Abba Joseph. The desert elder who answered Lot's what else with ten fingers lit like lamps.
Your line: all flame. Not a longer list, but a whole self, lit. Until tomorrow.

75.title: The mustard seed
75.hook: Kisa Gotami seeks medicine for her dead child from a house where no one has died (Therigatha commentary)
75.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers tell the story of Kisa Gotami in teaching on impermanence and grief, and she is honored as one of the enlightened nuns whose verses are kept in the Therigatha.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abba Joseph lifted fingers like ten lamps and told Lot he could become all flame. Your line was all flame.

Right after a loss, the world keeps moving, and that can feel wrong. People say things that don't help. A grieving person may go looking for the one thing, the one call or the one answer, that would undo it. In ancient India, a young mother named Kisa Gotami went looking for exactly that. The Buddhist texts remember her walk. It's a tender story, so i'll go slowly.
screen: `AFTER A LOSS.` → `LOOKING FOR THE ONE THING.` → `KISA GOTAMI'S WALK.`

segments.voice: Her name means something like Gotami the thin one. The story is told in the old Buddhist commentaries, on the poems of the early nuns and on the Dhammapada. She married and had a little boy. When he was just old enough to walk, he fell sick and died, and she couldn't accept it. She carried him on her hip from house to house in the city, asking everyone for medicine for her son. People turned away, or thought she had lost her mind. Finally someone sent her to the Buddha. He didn't argue. He didn't explain. He said: yes, I can help. Bring me a mustard seed, from a house where no one has ever died. Mustard seed was in every kitchen, the easiest thing in the world to ask for. So she went. At the first house: of course, take some. But we lost our father last year. At the next house, a daughter. Then a husband, a grandmother, a baby. Every door would give her the seed. No door could give her the seed she needed. Somewhere along that street, the story says, she understood. Death hadn't singled her out. It was in every house. She laid her son down, gently, came back to the Buddha, and later became a nun; her own verses are kept among the poems of the early nuns. He taught her not by arguing, but first with a walk, and a street of neighbors who knew her grief from the inside, and only then with a few words. Her sorrow wasn't taken away. She just wasn't alone in it anymore.
screen: `A MOTHER CARRIES HER SON.` · `BRING ONE MUSTARD SEED.` · `EVERY HOUSE HAS LOST SOMEONE.` · `SHE WASN'T ALONE IN IT.` · then, large: `NO HOUSE WITHOUT IT.`

segments.voice: If there's someone you've lost, let them come to mind gently, a face, a voice, a small ordinary moment, and if tears come, let them; if no one comes to mind, hold someone who's grieving. Then think of the other houses, on your street, in your town, in the world, where someone is remembering too, right now: your grief is yours, and it's also in good company. And if grief ever gets too heavy to carry alone, reach out: in the US you can call or text 988 at any hour, and wherever you are, help is there.
Kisa Gotami. A young mother whose grief sent her searching for a mustard seed from a home untouched by death.
Your line: no house without it. A small, kind word is enough. Day seventy-five, gently.

76.title: The poisoned arrow
76.hook: the Buddha: a wounded man won't wait to learn who shot him before the arrow comes out (Majjhima Nikaya 63)
76.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use the parable of the poisoned arrow to explain why the Buddha set aside certain metaphysical questions and focused on suffering and its ending.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kisa Gotami went door to door for a mustard seed and found no house without loss. Your line was no house without it.

Something goes wrong. The deal falls through, the diagnosis comes back, the text you didn't want arrives. And right away the questions come. Why did this happen? Whose fault is it? What does it mean about my life? Was it always going to go this way? Some of them matter. But while they're spinning, the actual hurt is still sitting there, untouched. The Buddha had a picture for this.
screen: `SOMETHING GOES WRONG.` → `WHY? WHOSE FAULT?` → `THE HURT, STILL UNTOUCHED.`

segments.voice: It's in the Middle Length Discourses, the Majjhima Nikaya, number sixty-three. A monk named Malunkyaputta is sitting alone, stewing. There are big questions the Buddha has never answered. Is the universe eternal, or not? Is it infinite, or not? Is the soul the same as the body? What happens to an awakened one after death? So he gives the Buddha an ultimatum: answer these, or I'm leaving. The Buddha starts with a question of his own: did I ever promise you I'd answer them? Then he tells a story. A man is shot with an arrow thickly smeared with poison. His friends and family rush to bring a surgeon. But the man says: no one pulls this arrow out until I know who shot me. Was he a noble, a priest, a merchant, a worker? What was his name, his family? Tall or short, dark or fair? What village? Was the bow a longbow or a crossbow? What was the string made of, and what feathers were on the arrow? That man, the Buddha says, would die before he learned any of it. He doesn't call the questions foolish. He says the holy life isn't built on answering them: they don't lead to calm, or to awakening. What he teaches instead is suffering, where it comes from, its ending, and the path to that ending: the wound, and how to heal it. Buddhist teachers read his silence on those questions in more than one way. But the order in the story is clear. First, the arrow comes out. The questions can come after, if they still seem urgent.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing that's hurting a little today, not the biggest, and notice the why questions that come with it: whose fault, what it means, how it happened. Set them to one side; they'll keep. Then ask a smaller question, what would help this hurt right now, a glass of water, an apology, a walk, a phone call, a rest, and picture doing it.
Salla. The Pali word for the arrow in the Buddha's picture of a wounded man who wants every answer before he'll let the surgeon help.
Your line: pull the arrow. The why can wait until the wound is tended. That's day seventy-six.

77.title: The Good Samaritan
77.hook: the man who stopped for the wounded traveler was the one nobody expected (Luke 10:25–37)
77.howItsDone: Christians read the Good Samaritan as Jesus's teaching on loving your neighbor, and churches, hospitals and charities around the world take the name for work that helps strangers in need.

segments.voice: Yesterday, salla: the poisoned arrow, and a man who wanted every answer before the surgeon could help. Your line was pull the arrow.

Here's a story so famous its name became an everyday word. Hospitals are named after it. There are laws named after it. And the person it's named for was the one nobody listening expected to be the hero. It ends a week of torches and arrows: Rabia's bucket, hands on an elephant in the dark, Abba Moses's leaking basket, fingers like lamps, a mother's mustard seed, an arrow that needed pulling. Sufi, Christian and Buddhist homes, each story kept by its own people.
screen: `A NAME ON HOSPITALS AND LAWS.` → `THE HERO NOBODY EXPECTED.` → `A WEEK OF TORCHES AND ARROWS.`

segments.voice: It's in the Gospel of Luke, chapter ten. An expert in the Jewish law asks Jesus what he must do to inherit eternal life. Jesus asks what the law says, and the lawyer answers with two commandments joined together: love God, and love your neighbor as yourself. Then he asks, as the King James puts it, "And who is my neighbour?" Jesus answers with a story. A man is going down the steep road from Jerusalem to Jericho. Robbers strip him, beat him, and leave him half dead. A priest sees him and "passed by on the other side." A Levite, a temple assistant, does the same. The text never says why. Then a Samaritan comes. Samaritans and Jews in that time had centuries of bad blood; each side had reasons to distrust the other. This Samaritan stops. He bandages the wounds, pouring on oil and wine, puts the man on his own animal, takes him to an inn, and pays the innkeeper two coins: whatever more it costs, I'll repay you when I come back. Then Jesus turns the question around. Not who counts as my neighbor, but which of these three acted like a neighbor? The lawyer answers: the one who showed him mercy. Jesus says, "Go, and do thou likewise." This is a Jewish teacher telling a Jewish lawyer a story built on the Jewish commandment to love your neighbor. It isn't a case against priests or Levites. Its surprise is that the helper came from the people the listeners least expected, and that being a neighbor is something you do, not something you're owed.
